newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Bosnian Serb pleads not guilty to genocide.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serb pleads not guilty to genocide.

text.p: A Bosnian Serb, accused of helping to set up camps in which Moslems and Croats were raped, tortured and killed, pleaded not guilty on Wednesday before the U.N. war crimes tribunal.
Milan Kovacevic, a 56-year-old hospital director, is the first person to appear before the tribunal in The Hague on a charge of genocide relating to the 1992-95 war in Bosnia.
He was seized on July 10 by soldiers of Britain's elite SAS, who shot dead another suspected Bosnian Serb war criminal on the same day for opening fire on them.
Kovacevic, walking slowly, was led into the high-tech court-room by two uniformed and armed United Nations guards.
Rising to his feet, he identified himself and confirmed to presiding judge Sir Ninian Stephen of Australia that he had understood the charges levelled against him by U.N. prosecutors.
"On the counts of this indictment, I am not guilty and, God and the justice of this court willing, I think I will be found not guilty," he said during a brief sitting.
Kovacevic is accused of helping set up camps where Moslems and Croats were rounded up during a brutal Serb "ethnic cleansing" campaign in northwest Bosnia in 1992.
The indictment described conditions in the Omarska, Keraterm and Trnopolje camps as appalling.

"Bosnian Serb military and police personnel in charge of these facilities, their staff and other persons...killed, sexually assaulted, tortured and otherwise physically and psychologically abused the detainees in the camps," it said.

"Detainees were continuously subjected to or forced to witness inhumane acts, including murder, rape and sexual assaults, torture, beatings and robbery, as well as other forms of mental and physical abuse."
Kovacevic sported a bushy moustache and wore a dark suit with an unbuttoned white shirt. He spoke in a low mumbling tone.
Before appearing in court Kovacevic had undergone medical tests. His lawyer, Igor Pantelic, said his client remained very ill with heart disease and had suffered several strokes.

Kovacevic and Simo Drljaca, the war crimes suspect shot by the British commandos, were described in the indictment as members of the Serb Crisis Staff in the Prijedor region which established and controlled the detention camps.
The operation to arrest them marked the first time that NATO-led troops in Bosnia had actively hunted down war crimes suspects, of whom more than 60 remain at large.
Bosnian Serb hardliners have since launched a retaliatory series of explosions against international peacekeepers.
Kovacevic and Drljaca were charged under sealed, or secret, indictments. These have unsettled allies of former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic who fear he may be arrested next.
Karadzic and his former military commander Ratko Mladic, both charged with genocide, head the tribunal's wanted list.
Kovacevic's initial appearance on Wednesday was a formality required under tribunal rules and his trial is not due to begin for at least several more months.
Judges, prosecutors and defence lawyers will meet to discuss the case on October 10 and Kovacevic will remain in a cell at the tribunal's detention centre in the meantime.
Created by the U.N. Security Council in May 1993, the tribunal has so far publicly indicted 78 suspects -- 57 Serbs, 18 Croats and three Moslems.
Two of these have been convicted and sentenced and a further eight are in the tribunal's custody. Two died before they could stand trial and the remaining 66 are still at large.
The tribunal is the first international body for the prosecution of war crimes since the Nuremberg and Tokyo trials, held in the aftermath of World War Two.
It has no police force of its own and relies on the former Yugoslav republics, other states or international troops in Bosnia to make arrests.
